label: Video Games
blurb: Playing them deliberately: systems worth studying, machines worth building, and the sideways exits into code and hardware.

nodes.label: Action RPGs
nodes.blurb: Loot, seasons and a passive tree with thousands of nodes. Played by people who enjoy the spreadsheet at least as much as the fighting.

nodes.label: Build Crafting
nodes.blurb: Planning a character on a huge skill tree before playing it. The hobby of reading a graph, which is roughly what this whole site is.

nodes.label: Roguelikes
nodes.blurb: Runs rather than saves. Losing is content, and the knowledge you keep between attempts is the actual progression.

nodes.label: Strategy Games
nodes.blurb: Turn based or grand. Long sessions, deep systems, and a community that writes more documentation than the developer did.

nodes.label: Speedrunning
nodes.blurb: Route planning, frame-level execution and a timer. A performance discipline built on top of somebody else's game.

nodes.label: Game Preservation
nodes.blurb: Dumping, documenting and keeping playable the things that are no longer sold. An archival hobby with a legal grey area attached.

nodes.label: Game Modding
nodes.blurb: Editing somebody's game with their tools, or without them. The most common first programming project people actually finish.

nodes.label: Game Development
nodes.blurb: Making a small one rather than modding a big one. Scope control is the whole skill and almost nobody has it on the first try.

nodes.label: Playing With Friends
nodes.blurb: The scheduled evening that keeps a friend group in contact. Often the only hobby on this map with a fixed weekly slot.

nodes.label: Controller Modding
nodes.blurb: Hall effect sticks, arcade sticks and custom buttons. A soldering hobby that hides inside a gaming one.

nodes.label: PC Building
nodes.blurb: Parts picking, cable routing and thermals. Assembling is the easy half; deciding what to buy is where the research goes.

nodes.label: Sim Racing
nodes.blurb: Wheel, pedals and a rig bolted together. The gear escalation is steep and the physics knowledge transfers to a real track.

nodes.label: Flight Simulation
nodes.blurb: Procedures, charts and a cockpit built out of switch panels. Closer to a study hobby than to a game.

nodes.label: In-Game Photography
nodes.blurb: Composition, focal length and light inside a rendered world. Every skill transfers except the walking around.

nodes.label: JRPGs
nodes.blurb: Sixty-hour stories, turn-based menus and a party you pick favourites from. The backlog is the real endgame, and everyone in the genre is losing to it.

nodes.label: Fighting Games
nodes.blurb: Frame data, spacing and a training mode that never lies. The one genre where improvement is measured against a person who is trying to stop you.

nodes.label: Rhythm Games
nodes.blurb: Notes fall and you hit them on time, graded to the millisecond. Practice looks exactly like playing, which no instrument has managed.

nodes.label: Online Worlds
nodes.blurb: One persistent world, thousands of strangers and a raid calendar. The only games on this map that carry on without you while you sleep.

nodes.label: VR and Simulation
nodes.blurb: A headset, a cleared floor and a cable you learn to step over. Nobody believes it until the demo, and nobody explains it well afterwards either.

edges.note: The tree is the game for a lot of people. Hours go into planning a character that is never actually played.
Modding gives you the hard parts already solved, which is why more people finish a mod than finish a game.
Two answers to the same RPG root: one turns combat into menus, the other into a spreadsheet. Plenty of people keep a save in both.
The genre never really left the couch. Netcode caught up, but the local with a borrowed stick is still the front door.
Dance pads, drum kits and hand-built sliders. Half the scene ends up soldering the controller the arcade had.
The weekly session, scaled up to a guild and written into a raid calendar.
Head tracking is the one upgrade both cockpits agree on. Depth perception is why the landings improve.
